title: Offline AI-powered scribe: Reducing documentation burden in underserved healthcare settings
authors: reddy ch, deekshith; Sharma, Dr.Pooja
abstract: Introduction Clinical documentation is the backbone of modern healthcare, ensuring that each encounter between patient and physician is recorded with accuracy, completeness, and clarity. In an era of rapidly expanding patient populations, increasingly complex chronic diseases, and escalating demands for quality metrics, documentation has evolved into more than a clinical necessity: it has become a determinant of healthcare outcomes, institutional performance, and physician well-being. However, the process of documenting patient encounters remains a formidable burden on clinicians, consuming disproportionate amounts of time and often interfering with the central mission of medicine — direct patient care. The last decade has seen the rise of electronic medical records (EMRs) and, more recently, the introduction of AI-enabled cloud-based scribe technologies that promise to reduce this burden. Yet these solutions remain unevenly distributed, prohibitively expensive for resource-limited systems, and reliant on infrastructure that excludes vast populations of patients and physicians globally. The result is a paradox: while the technology to ease documentation exists, its benefits are disproportionately concentrated in wealthy institutions, widening the inequity gap in healthcare delivery. This project seeks to address that gap through the design and development of “Streamline Scribe” , an offline, AI-powered, privacy-first medical scribing prototype. Built with open-source, on-device tools such as Vosk speech-to-text and Tesseract OCR, the system enables clinicians to generate structured H&P, SOAP, and discharge notes without internet connectivity, cloud dependencies, or recurring subscription costs. By embedding principles of accessibility, equity, and user-centered design, this innovation represents a new paradigm: bringing advanced AI functionality to the very frontlines of global healthcare, where connectivity is unreliable, budgets are constrained, and clinical time is at its scarcest. Background Physician burnout has reached epidemic proportions worldwide. In the United States alone, surveys estimate that physicians spend nearly twice as much time on administrative tasks and documentation as they do on direct patient care. Studies published in Annals of Internal Medicine estimate an average of 1–2 hours of clerical work per hour of clinical care , often extending into late evenings — what is colloquially referred to as “pajama time.” For residents and trainees, the burden is even more acute, with documentation serving as both a learning tool and a source of stress, frequently stretching daily work hours far beyond clinical schedules. Global inequities exacerbate this challenge. In high-income countries, AI-enabled scribe tools such as Nuance DAX, Abridge, and Suki are increasingly adopted by enterprise hospital systems, offering real-time transcription, summarization, and structured note generation. Yet these systems rely on cloud infrastructure, stable broadband, and significant subscription costs , making them inaccessible to community hospitals, residency clinics, rural practices, and health missions abroad. Physicians in underserved regions remain dependent on manual note-taking, risking incomplete documentation, reduced continuity of care, and poor patient outcomes. Privacy concerns further complicate adoption. Uploading sensitive patient data to cloud servers introduces risks of breaches, compliance failures with HIPAA or GDPR, and ethical concerns around secondary data use. While enterprise systems may mitigate these risks with robust contracts and encryption, individual clinicians or smaller organizations often lack such safeguards, leaving them vulnerable to security gaps. In parallel, academic medicine and global health missions continue to emphasize the importance of low-cost, scalable, and equitable innovations that serve the needs of the many rather than the privileged few. Documentation — though often overlooked compared to flashy imaging or therapeutic technologies — is at the heart of this challenge. Without robust records, continuity of care breaks down, quality metrics cannot be tracked, research datasets cannot be validated, and patients themselves lose agency in their health journey. Thus, there exists both a clinical imperative and a moral responsibility : to develop documentation solutions that are accessible, affordable, offline, and equitable, while maintaining the standards of accuracy and security that modern healthcare demands. Problem Statement The problem addressed by this project is threefold: Documentation Burden on Clinicians Physicians, residents, and medical students worldwide face a crippling documentation workload. A single inpatient admission note may require 2–4 hours of detailed typing, copying, formatting, and verifying data across multiple EMR tabs. Outpatient notes, while shorter, accumulate into hundreds daily across busy clinics. This burden detracts from face-to-face patient interaction, diminishes physician satisfaction, and contributes to burnout. Inequitable Access to AI Tools The most advanced scribe tools are concentrated in resource-rich settings, with costs ranging from hundreds to thousands of dollars per month per physician. These tools rely on constant high-speed internet, excluding entire regions of the world where connectivity is intermittent, unstable, or unavailable. As a result, healthcare workers in underserved areas are left behind, perpetuating global health inequities. Privacy and Compliance Risks Cloud-based transcription requires uploading patient voice data, images, or EMR snippets to external servers. Even when anonymized, this practice raises concerns regarding patient consent, regulatory compliance, and secondary use of data for commercial purposes. Many physicians and institutions hesitate to adopt such tools, fearing reputational and legal risks. Objectives Against this backdrop, the Streamline Scribe project was initiated with the following objectives: Develop a fully offline, on-device AI documentation prototype that can transform speech and images into structured clinical notes without requiring internet access. Ensure privacy and security by design , through PHI masking, local processing, and export options limited to the clinician’s device. Enhance accessibility and equity by utilizing open-source software (Vosk, Tesseract) and low-cost deployment models that can operate on basic hardware available to most clinics worldwide. Validate functionality in simulated encounters , focusing on metrics of documentation time, transcription accuracy, clinician fatigue, and patient interaction. Bridge innovation with education and global health , positioning the prototype as a tool not only for frontline clinicians but also for medical students, residents, and global health workers engaged in underserved communities. Create a scalable foundation for future iterations , including multilingual transcription, EMR integration, and advanced AI summarization models, while maintaining the principles of equity and offline operabilityMethods and Prototype Architecture The development of the Streamline Scribe prototype was guided by principles of privacy-first architecture, modular design, and real-world usability . The system was built from the ground up to operate on-device, requiring no internet connection, and relying exclusively on open-source tools to maximize accessibility and adaptability. 1. System Components The prototype integrates five core components: Speech-to-Text (STT) with Vosk Vosk is a lightweight, offline speech recognition toolkit capable of running on laptops and even smartphones with minimal processing power. It supports multiple languages and can transcribe speech in real time. For clinical contexts, we tested domain-specific vocabulary additions (e.g., “atrial fibrillation,” “HbA1c,” “thyroidectomy”) to improve accuracy. Optical Character Recognition (OCR) with Tesseract Tesseract OCR was incorporated to capture data from images, lab slips, or scanned documents. This feature allows clinicians in resource-limited settings to digitize handwritten or printed notes and integrate them seamlessly into structured documentation. Structured Template Generation We designed modular templates for common clinical formats: H&P (History & Physical Exam) SOAP (Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan) Discharge Summaries Templates were built with flexibility, allowing clinicians to dictate freely while the system auto-populates structured fields. Privacy Safeguards The prototype employs PHI masking tools , including face-blurring for patient images and automatic redaction of personal identifiers. All data processing occurs locally, ensuring compliance with HIPAA and GDPR principles. Export Options Clinicians can export completed notes in TXT or PDF formats with one click. Exported files remain on the device, avoiding reliance on cloud storage or third-party services. 2. Workflow The documentation workflow was designed to mirror natural physician behavior while reducing cognitive and clerical load. Encounter Initiation The physician launches the application and selects the template type (H&P, SOAP, discharge). Data Capture Speech Input : Physicians dictate directly into the device’s microphone. Real-time transcription displays on screen, enabling immediate correction. Image Input : Supporting documents or images (lab slips, consult notes) are captured via webcam or uploaded as files. OCR converts these into editable text. Auto-Structuring The system parses dictated or scanned content into the correct sections of the chosen template. For example, “patient complains of chest pain” is automatically placed under Subjective , while “EKG shows ST elevation” is categorized under Objective . Privacy Review Before finalizing, the system highlights any potentially sensitive identifiers for clinician approval or redaction. Export and Save Notes are exported locally in preferred formats. Clinicians can copy-paste into EMRs, print for patient records, or store securely on their device. 3. Simulation Environment To evaluate the prototype, we simulated 20 outpatient encounters covering common conditions: hypertension, diabetes, hypothyroidism, COPD, and depression. Each encounter was enacted by two participants — one playing the clinician and the other the patient — to mimic natural dialogue, interruptions, and pacing. We collected data on: Documentation Time (start to final export) Transcription Accuracy (compared to manually prepared reference transcripts) Clinician Fatigue (self-reported on a Likert scale) Patient Interaction Quality (evaluated by observer, rated on attention and eye contact) 4. Metrics and Definitions Documentation Time Reduction : Calculated as percentage decrease relative to baseline manual note entry in Microsoft Word or EMR mock-up. Transcription Accuracy : Ratio of correctly transcribed words/phrases to total spoken words, with focus on medical terminology. Fatigue Scores : Clinician participants rated their mental fatigue after each encounter on a scale of 1 (none) to 5 (severe). Patient Interaction Quality : Independent observers scored whether clinicians maintained eye contact, responded to patient cues, and avoided screen distraction. 5. Iterative Feedback and Refinement Each simulation session was followed by debrief interviews with participants. Feedback themes included: The need for hotkey-based corrections during transcription. Desire for multilingual support for patient instructions. Request for voice commands (e.g., “new paragraph,” “insert vitals”). Improvements in medical vocabulary recognition , particularly for abbreviations. Based on feedback, we added: Custom medical dictionary integration into Vosk. Basic voice command recognition for formatting. Template auto-fill shortcuts , such as inserting common exam findings. 6. Technical Requirements The prototype was built to run on widely available hardware: Minimum Specs : 4GB RAM, Intel i3 or equivalent, 128GB storage. Operating Systems : Windows, Linux, MacOS. Optional Add-ons : USB microphone for clearer transcription, webcam for OCR. By designing for low system requirements, the tool remains usable in rural clinics, residency settings with limited infrastructure, and field missions with only basic laptops. 7. Ethical Considerations Even though the prototype operates offline, ethical safeguards were prioritized: Informed Consent Simulation : In real-world deployment, patients would be informed that dictation is being transcribed via an AI tool. Data Retention : No data leaves the clinician’s device unless deliberately exported. Bias Mitigation : Efforts were made to diversify training data for medical terms to reduce transcription errors for non-English accents. Results (Preview for Next Section) Preliminary outcomes from the simulations demonstrated: 80% reduction in documentation time (average: 60 minutes → 12 minutes per patient). 95% transcription accuracy post-minimal correction, with significant improvement when medical dictionaries were added. 90% of participants reported reduced fatigue compared to manual typing. Observers noted improved patient interaction in 85% of encounters, as clinicians were less distracted by screens. Results & Findings The Streamline Scribe prototype was evaluated across 20 simulated outpatient encounters. Each encounter tested the system’s ability to transcribe, structure, and export clinical documentation efficiently while preserving privacy and enhancing clinician–patient interaction. 1. Documentation Efficiency Baseline documentation, performed through manual typing into Microsoft Word or EMR mock-ups, required an average of 55–65 minutes per patient encounter , depending on case complexity. Using the prototype, average time dropped to 12 minutes , representing an 80% reduction in clerical workload Results & Findings The Streamline Scribe prototype was evaluated across 20 simulated outpatient encounters. Each encounter tested the system’s ability to transcribe, structure, and export clinical documentation efficiently while preserving privacy and enhancing clinician–patient interaction. 1. Documentation Efficiency Baseline documentation, performed through manual typing into Microsoft Word or EMR mock-ups, required an average of 55–65 minutes per patient encounter , depending on case complexity. Using the prototype, average time dropped to 12 minutes , representing an 80% reduction in clerical workload . Baseline (Manual Entry): H&P: 65 minutes SOAP: 55 minutes Discharge Summary: 60 minutes Prototype (AI-Enhanced): H&P: 13 minutes SOAP: 11 minutes Discharge Summary: 12 minutes This reduction translated to over 5 hours saved per day for a clinician seeing 6–8 patients, suggesting the potential to dramatically alleviate documentation burden. 2. Transcription Accuracy Speech recognition performance was a critical metric. Raw Vosk transcription produced ~85% accuracy with general vocabulary. After integrating a customized medical dictionary (including terms such as “myocardial infarction,” “HbA1c,” “thyroidectomy,” and “neutropenia”), accuracy improved to 95% with minimal corrections . Errors were most common with: Rare syndromes (e.g., “Bardet–Biedl”). Abbreviations (e.g., “CABG” misread as “cabbage”). Drug names with phonetic overlap. Despite this, corrections were minimal and required less than 3 minutes per note. 3. Patient Interaction Observers recorded significant improvements in patient–clinician dynamics: 85% of encounters demonstrated increased eye contact and attentiveness. Clinicians reported feeling “freer” to engage with patients without needing to stare at a screen. Patients responded positively, with mock patients noting that they “felt listened to.” This highlights a key advantage of offline AI scribes: not just time saved, but restoration of human connection in clinical care. 4. Clinician Fatigue Self-reported fatigue scores (scale 1–5): Manual Documentation: Average 4.3 (high fatigue). Prototype-Assisted Documentation: Average 2.0 (low fatigue). Clinicians emphasized that repetitive typing and screen focus contributed most to fatigue, while dictation and structured automation reduced cognitive load. 5. Privacy & Offline Reliability The offline design proved robust: 100% of encounters were completed without internet connectivity. PHI safeguards (token redaction, face blur) operated as expected. No sensitive data was transmitted externally, ensuring compliance with privacy principles. This differentiates Streamline Scribe from most commercial AI scribes, which rely on cloud-based infrastructure and raise concerns around HIPAA/GDPR compliance. 6. User Feedback Key insights from clinician participants: Positive: “It feels like the EMR finally works for me, not against me.” “I could imagine using this on global health missions where connectivity is poor.” “For residency clinics, this would save hours of late-night charting.” Areas for Improvement: Voice command system needed refinement. Desire for integration with EMRs (e.g., Epic, Athena). Support for non-English dictation (e.g., Spanish, Hindi) for multilingual care. 7. Comparative Evaluation We benchmarked Streamline Scribe against three commercial scribe solutions (names omitted for neutrality). Commercial Scribes: Accuracy: 97–99% Cost: $300–500/month per clinician Requires continuous internet access Cloud storage with potential PHI risks Streamline Scribe: Accuracy: 95% (with corrections) Cost: open-source, <$50 setup Offline, full local control PHI masking and no data export Although commercial tools achieved slightly higher accuracy, Streamline Scribe outperformed on cost, privacy, and accessibility , making it uniquely positioned for resource-limited settings. 8. Broader Implications The evaluation demonstrated not only feasibility but also system-level potential : For Residency Clinics: Reduced after-hours charting, mitigating burnout. For Global Health Missions: Portable, offline design enables deployment in rural India, Sub-Saharan Africa, or refugee camps. For Primary Care in the U.S.: Restores face-to-face connection in 15-minute visits burdened by EMR clicks. For Policy Makers: Demonstrates that AI innovation can be equitable , not just enterprise-focused. 9. Limitations Despite promising results, several limitations were acknowledged: Small Sample Size: Only 20 encounters; broader trials are needed. Simulated Patients: Real-world variability may introduce more transcription challenges. Limited Integration: Currently operates as standalone; does not auto-populate EMRs. Medical Vocabulary Gaps: Rare conditions and polypharmacy terms require further tuning. User Training: Some clinicians needed 1–2 sessions to adapt to dictation workflows. 10. Future Directions The project laid a foundation for scalable innovation. Next steps include: Expanded Clinical Trials: Pilot testing in residency clinics and rural hospitals. Multilingual Support: Training models for major global languages. Seamless EMR Integration: APIs to link with Epic, Cerner, Athena, and open-source EMRs. Advanced AI Modules: Incorporating large language models (LLMs) offline for summarization and decision support. User-Centered Design: Continuous feedback loops with clinicians to refine usability. Summary of Findings The Streamline Scribe prototype validated its central hypothesis: equitable, efficient, and private AI documentation is possible without cloud infrastructure . Key outcomes: 80% reduction in documentation time. 95% transcription accuracy with medical vocabulary support. 90% of clinicians reported decreased fatigue. 85% of encounters showed improved patient interaction. 100% offline functionality preserved privacy and accessibility. These results demonstrate that innovations in clinical informatics can be scaled beyond enterprise systems , empowering physicians in both advanced healthcare systems and underserved global settingsDiscussion & Impact The evaluation of Streamline Scribe demonstrates more than just a technical proof-of-concept. It highlights the transformative potential of accessible AI in reshaping healthcare documentation across diverse settings. By bridging gaps between high-resource and low-resource environments, the project provides a framework for equitable innovation in clinical practice. 1. Rethinking Documentation Burden For decades, documentation has been a silent driver of physician burnout. Studies consistently show that for every one hour of patient care, clinicians may spend nearly two additional hours completing EMR-related tasks. This imbalance is particularly severe in primary care, where short visits must address complex conditions while also meeting administrative requirements. Streamline Scribe reframes this dynamic. By reducing documentation time by nearly 80% , the prototype demonstrates that technological interventions need not add complexity; they can simplify. Unlike enterprise EMRs that often increase workload, this system aligns with the natural flow of a clinical encounter—listening, recording, summarizing, and exporting. The broader implication is that burnout is not inevitable . With thoughtful design, tools can restore balance, allowing clinicians to focus on healing rather than typing. 2. Human Connection as a Clinical Metric Perhaps the most striking outcome was the improvement in patient interaction . While efficiency gains are critical, the quality of physician–patient relationships defines the essence of medicine. Observers noted that clinicians using the prototype were more present, engaged, and empathetic. Patients reported feeling heard—a metric often overlooked in technological evaluations. This finding suggests that the future of clinical AI must be judged not only on accuracy and cost, but also on its ability to strengthen human connection . By restoring eye contact and freeing clinicians from screens, Streamline Scribe advances the core values of medicine: trust, compassion, and presence. 3. Equity in Global Healthcare Most commercial AI scribes target enterprise hospitals and charge subscription fees that exclude community clinics, residency programs, and resource-limited nations. By contrast, Streamline Scribe was intentionally designed to operate offline, on low-cost hardware, without subscription fees . This makes it uniquely suited for: Residency Clinics: Where budgets are limited, and residents often struggle with overwhelming documentation. Rural U.S. Clinics: Where internet connectivity may be unreliable, and patient loads are high. Global Health Missions: Where cloud-based tools are impractical, but privacy and efficiency are equally vital. In this way, the project embodies the principle of equitable innovation —ensuring that AI’s benefits are not confined to privileged healthcare systems but extend to the most underserved populations. 4. Educational & Scholarly Value Beyond clinical application, Streamline Scribe revealed unexpected value in education and research . Structured outputs (H&P, SOAP, discharge notes) created uniform case materials that were easily de-identified for teaching. This allowed for: Standardized case discussions in residency settings. Quality improvement analysis using consistent documentation formats. Research opportunities where de-identified notes could be aggregated to study documentation workflows. This scholarly dimension enabled the project to be presented at multiple academic venues (AMIA, IEEE-BHI, Stanford-BHA, AI-Health), strengthening its credibility and contributing directly to the ERAS CV under research, innovation, and scholarly activity . 5. Limitations as a Source of Growth While results were promising, limitations underscored the iterative nature of innovation: Limited Vocabulary: Certain rare syndromes and drug names challenged recognition. Small-Scale Evaluation: Larger trials with real-world patients are required. Integration Gaps: Without direct EMR integration, clinicians still required manual transfer of notes. Training Curve: Some participants needed orientation to dictation-based workflows. These limitations, however, are opportunities for refinement . Addressing them through collaboration with physicians, informatics experts, and technologists will ensure that the next version of Streamline Scribe is even more robust and scalable. 6. Implications for U.S. Residency Training For residency programs, the significance of this project extends beyond technology: it demonstrates the applicant’s capacity for innovation under pressure . Following a Step 2 setback, the project served as a tangible example of resilience, turning adversity into growth. By building and showcasing a functional prototype within weeks, the work reflects creativity, adaptability, and scholarly initiative. Collaboration with faculty such as Dr. Pooja Sharma highlights the ability to engage mentors, seek feedback, and translate ideas into academic output. For program directors, this narrative signals not only academic readiness but also leadership potential in clinical informatics —a field increasingly vital to the future of medicine. 7. Bridging Innovation and Primary Care Streamline Scribe also embodies the dual focus of your professional aspirations: clinical care and informatics . As a future internist or family physician, the tool reflects your commitment to continuity of care , by ensuring more time for conversations and relationship-building. As an innovator, it highlights your vision of leveraging AI to extend care delivery in both U.S. and global contexts. This synergy demonstrates that technology and empathy are not opposing forces; they can be mutually reinforcing pillars of modern medical practice. 8. Broader Policy & Ethical Considerations The project also opens conversation about AI ethics in healthcare : Privacy: Offline, local-first design ensures PHI remains within clinician control, unlike cloud models. Equity: Low-cost deployment prevents a digital divide where only wealthy systems benefit. Sustainability: Open-source design reduces dependency on proprietary vendors. In an era of growing mistrust of big-tech solutions, Streamline Scribe offers a model for responsible innovation —technology built not for profit margins but for physician well-being and patient dignity. 9. Future Vision Looking forward, the project positions you to continue leading innovation: Clinical Goal: Become a primary care physician (IM/FM) who provides continuity, dignity, and long-term care for chronic illnesses. Informatics Goal: Expand AI tools like Streamline Scribe to help physicians globally, reducing burnout and improving quality of care. Scholarly Goal: Mentor students and residents in combining bedside skills with technological literacy, building a new generation of physician-innovators. In short, the project reflects a visionary trajectory : caring for patients today while shaping the tools of tomorrow. Conclusion of Discussion The evaluation of Streamline Scribe underscores its dual contribution: Immediate impact —reducing documentation burden, improving patient interaction, and preserving privacy. Long-term potential —scaling equitable innovation globally, reshaping primary care, and training the next generation of physicians. For residency applications, it demonstrates resilience, creativity, leadership, and empathy—qualities that define not only a strong applicant but a future leader in medicineConclusion & Full Integration The journey of developing Streamline Scribe has been more than the creation of a tool; it has been a personal and professional proving ground. At its core, this project is not just about efficiency, but about reimagining what medicine can look like when technology and empathy converge . 1. A Story of Resilience and Innovation The origin of this project lies in resilience. After facing setbacks in the path toward U.S. residency, instead of retreating, I channeled adversity into creation. The decision to build a prototype under pressure was not accidental—it was deliberate proof that challenges could be catalysts for growth. This resilience resonates with residency programs: the ability to face obstacles, reframe them, and emerge stronger is precisely the skill physicians need when confronted with the unpredictable realities of patient care. Streamline Scribe is thus more than a prototype; it is a living example of adaptability in action . 2. Clinical Foundation with Scholarly Output The clinical grounding of the project ensured it was not a speculative exercise. By testing the prototype in simulated outpatient encounters and documenting physician fatigue, transcription accuracy, and patient interaction, the work was tied directly to real-world outcomes . From this foundation, the project generated academic output : Abstracts submitted to AMIA, IEEE-BHI, AI-Health, and Stanford-BHA , Presentations in clinical documentation and health informatics forums , Recognition from mentors like Dr. Pooja Sharma, who saw the tool’s educational and scholarly potential. In this way, a single innovation multiplied into research, mentorship, and professional growth—demonstrating the synergy between clinical practice and academic inquiry . 3. Lessons in Human Connection One of the most profound lessons of the project was the realization that technology can restore humanity to medicine . Far too often, clinicians are trapped behind computer screens, robbed of eye contact, and unable to engage fully with their patients. Streamline Scribe flipped this script. Observers reported that clinicians using the prototype were more present, more attentive, and more engaged. Patients expressed that they felt listened to. This reaffirmed that the true value of innovation lies not in faster charts , but in stronger human connection . As a physician-in-training, this lesson is deeply personal. My earliest patient encounter—a 26-year-old woman whose life was cut short not by disease but by stigma—taught me that listening can be as powerful as prescribing . Streamline Scribe embodies that philosophy: every technical detail is aimed at enabling physicians to listen more and type less. 4. Equity and Accessibility In medicine, access determines outcomes. Commercial AI scribes often remain inaccessible to the very clinicians who need them most—those in residency clinics, rural practices, or global health missions. By making Streamline Scribe offline, low-cost, and privacy-first, the project challenges the idea that innovation must be exclusive. This reflects a broader ethical commitment: that technology in healthcare should not deepen inequality but bridge it. For residency directors, this positions me not only as a trainee with technical curiosity but also as someone who views innovation through the lens of justice and service . 5. Integration into Professional Identity The impact of Streamline Scribe extends beyond the prototype itself. It has shaped my professional identity in three key ways: As a clinician: I see patients not only as cases but as individuals with fears, dignity, and hopes. Technology is a tool to empower—not replace—that connection. As a scholar: I view every clinical challenge as a potential question, every inefficiency as an opportunity for research, and every patient encounter as a chance to generate insight. As an innovator: I believe in building tools that are not only cutting-edge but also scalable, ethical, and equitable . This integration ensures that residency is not the end point of my growth but the launchpad for lifelong contribution . 6. Preparing for Residency and Beyond Residency demands more than knowledge; it demands endurance, collaboration, and vision . Streamline Scribe prepared me in ways that mirror residency itself: Endurance: Long hours coding, testing, and refining mirrored the stamina required in clinical training. Collaboration: Working with mentors, co-authors, and peers reflected the teamwork of multidisciplinary care. Vision: Thinking beyond immediate results to long-term implications trained me to see beyond symptoms to systems. This alignment reassures program directors that I bring not only the empathy of a clinician but also the vision of a problem-solver who can contribute to the evolution of medical practice. 7. Future Work Streamline Scribe is a foundation, not a finished product. Future directions include: Integration with EMRs to eliminate manual transfer, making adoption seamless. Expanding vocabulary libraries to cover rare syndromes and medications. Mobile deployment for rural clinics and global missions. Collaborative trials across residency programs to validate impact on learning, burnout, and patient satisfaction. These goals ensure the project continues to evolve, aligning with the values of innovation, adaptability, and continuous improvement—precisely the ethos that residency training cultivates. 8. Symbolism for My Journey Ultimately, Streamline Scribe symbolizes my broader journey. Just as it reduces clutter from documentation, my own path has been about stripping away noise —from bullying, stigma, and setbacks—and focusing on clarity of purpose. Just as it preserves patient dignity, my own mission is to ensure that medicine honors dignity at every stage of care. Just as it thrives without the cloud, my own growth has often come without privilege or infrastructure , relying instead on resilience, creativity, and discipline. This alignment makes the project not only a technical innovation but also a personal metaphor for the kind of physician I aspire to be. Final Conclusion Streamline Scribe is not just an offline AI prototype. It is: A tool that reduces documentation by 80%, preserves privacy, and strengthens patient connection. A scholarly project that generated abstracts, collaborations, and academic recognition. A personal testament to resilience, discipline, and innovation under pressure. A visionary model for equitable healthcare innovation in the U.S. and globally. As I stand on the threshold of residency, I bring with me this journey: the empathy born from patient encounters, the discipline forged through personal transformation, and the creativity proven through innovation. My aspiration is clear: to serve as a physician who heals both body and spirit, while contributing to systems that make care more humane and accessible. Residency will give me the platform to deepen my skills, expand my vision, and collaborate with mentors and colleagues to make that aspiration a reality. Streamline Scribe is just the beginning of this path—a signpost of the physician I aim to become and the future of medicine I want to help shape.

abstract: UNSTRUCTURED Widespread implementation of ambient artificial intelligence (AI) scribe technologies in the United States and globally continues to outpace available evidence on learning and cognition in medical education and practice. authors: Sushma HR; null Ramesha
abstract: The development of Artificial Intelligence has led to a revolution in the field of Library and Information Science and the Indian Knowledge System. This is because the introduction of AI technology has improved the preservation, management, and dissemination of information resources. The IKS has developed over many years through ancient scriptures, oral history, and documents. The Indian Knowledge System is one of the most enriched intellectual heritage systems that needs to be preserved. This research paper uses a qualitative, analytical method to examine the effects of AI on Library and Information Sciences, including the Indian Knowledge System. This research paper examines how AI techniques such as OCR, NLP, machine learning, and automated indexing can improve access to the legacy knowledge system. The study discusses the specific needs and the various applications of AI technologies into LIS and IKS by improving the digitisation, preservation, retrieval, and accessibility of traditional knowledge. However, the study identifies the challenges, including data privacy concerns, the need for skilled professionals, and the risk of algorithmic bias. The paper concludes that, despite of these challenges, the integration of AI in LIS holds strong potential to transform the management of traditional knowledge systems, strengthen the global visibility of the Indian Knowledge System and foster deeper understanding and appreciation of its intellectual heritage.

authors: Guilherme Sacchi de Camargo Correia; Rami Manochakian; Reema Tawfiq; Eric Kumar Singhi; Dena Rhinehart; Govind Warrier; Kristen A. Marrone; Talha Badar; Anand P. Jillella; Rahul Gosain; Rohit Gosain; Douglas B. Flora; Muhamad Alhaj Moustafa
abstract: e13677 Background: The development of AI led to the emergence of tools such as AIS, which have been increasingly adopted in medicine. However, formal evaluation of barriers and clinical care gaps in HemOnc is limited, particularly regarding treatment plan complexities and toxicity documentation. Methods: Structured investigator-developed surveys about AIS availability, adoption, benefits, and challenges were developed on Qualtrics and approved by the IRB. HemOnc faculty physicians (FP), advanced practice providers (APP), and trainees (HOT) were surveyed between 11/14/25-1/16/26. Surveys were distributed in the USA via email, social media (on X), and ASCO myConnection. Descriptive statistics were used for analysis. Results: 132 participants responded to the survey: 55 FP (42%), 14 APP (11%), and 63 HOT (48%). 80% of them reported having AIS at their institutions, and 54% of those reported using these tools in their clinical practice. Among FP and APP, 72% practiced in academic settings, 14% in community, and 13% in hybrid centers. Among those not using AIS, identified barriers were issues with note formatting (56%), lack of training (25%), and concerns that the note content is incorrect or inadequate (25%). 60% are willing to use AIS if note formatting matched their preference, and 42% would try it if contents better reflected the patient encounter. Table 1 details the proportion of encounters using AIS, the portion of documentation it was used for, and the perceived challenges with these tools. Among AIS users, the average satisfaction score was 5.3 on a 7 point scale, corresponding to participants being somewhat satisfied. Participants agreed slightly that AIS had reduced their feeling of work-related burnout, with an average score of 3.6 on a 5 point scale. Overall, participants felt neutral about how well-suited AIS are for HemOnc, with an average score of 4.0 on a 7 point scale. Conclusions: Despite AIS being widely available, 46% of the surveyed HemOnc workforce do not use them in clinical practice. Those who do reported decreased time spent on documentation outside work hours and a slight reduction in the feeling of burnout. Formatting issues and record integration remain barriers, with substantial concerns about AIS not adequately describing HemOnc treatment plans. To bridge the last mile of integration into HemOnc, partnership between AIS developers and the clinical workforce is essential to meet clinical needs, while prioritizing patient safety and data privacy. title: Teaching Clinicians to Speak AI: A Novel Approach to Prompt Engineering for Medical Scribe Technology (Preprint)
authors: Alex Bendersky
abstract: BACKGROUND Physical therapy, like other sectors of U.S. healthcare, faces increasing documentation burden and growing demand for patient-centered care. AI scribes offer a promising solution by automating clinical documentation, but their effectiveness depends heavily on clinicians’ ability to guide these systems through well-designed prompts. Currently, physical therapists lack structured training in this competency. OBJECTIVE This Viewpoint introduces and standardizes the SCRIBE Framework, a systematic, six-step approach to prompt engineering, designed to help physical therapists use AI scribes effectively, ethically, and safely. METHODS The framework was developed through synthesis of literature on prompt engineering, healthcare AI adoption, and documentation standards in rehabilitation. It was refined for relevance to clinical workflows in physical therapy and allied health professions. RESULTS The SCRIBE Framework outlines six practical steps for prompt design: Set the Specialist Role, Clarify Context and Sources, Require Structured Response, Include Clinical Logic, Build in Boundaries, and Establish Voice and Style. Together, these steps enable therapists to create prompts that generate accurate, compliant, and clinically valid documentation. The framework addresses efficiency, ethical risks, and professional communication standards. CONCLUSIONS The integration of AI scribes into physical therapy is inevitable. Prompt engineering represents a new professional competency that shifts therapists from passive users to active conductors of AI documentation. Adoption of the SCRIBE Framework can reduce administrative burden, enhance clinical accuracy, and ensure that AI technologies support patient-centered care in ways that are sustainable and ethically sound.

title: AI in medical practice: doctors’ perspective on the benefits, challenges and facilitators of artificial intelligence scribe use
authors: Jessica L. Irons; Andreas Duenser; Tracy Pickett; Georgina Haysom; Melanie J. McGrath
abstract: Abstract Purpose As artificial intelligence (AI) scribes become more common in clinical settings, understanding the human factors influencing their uptake is critical. This study investigates doctors’ perceptions of AI scribes, focusing on their benefits, challenges (risks or barriers) and facilitators of scribe use in medical practice. Methods We conducted focus groups with thirty-three medical practitioners (21 general practitioners and 12 medical specialists). Separate groups were conducted for AI scribe users and non-users. Benefits, challenges, and facilitators of AI scribe use were identified through researcher-coded qualitative analysis and synthesised into overarching themes. Results AI users had positive perceptions of scribes, reporting improvements to efficiency, quality of notes and doctor-patient interactions. The major challenge themes emerging across AI users and non-users were (1) insufficient knowledge about AI technology and data management, (2) errors produced by scribes, (3) medico-legal risks and responsibilities, (4) privacy concerns, (5) overreliance and de-skilling and (6) doctors losing control over decisions. Perceived facilitators to overcome these challenges included guidance on AI scribe best practice, regulation of AI technology, peer learning and the development of new skills and workflows for using AI. Conclusions Doctors in this study saw promise in AI scribes reducing their administrative burden and streamlining clinical documentation. However, AI errors, limited knowledge of the technology and data management, and fears about how AI might change clinical work are significant barriers for some doctors. Clear policy and guidance from leading medical bodies, as well as ongoing research on real-world implementation, will play an important role in supporting responsible adoption in medical practice.

title: Evaluating Provider Experience and Practice Impact of AI Scribe Implementation Across an Ontario Health Team
authors: Somers, Ali; Glatt, Daniel
abstract: Background: The integration of AI-powered scribe technology offers potential solutions to reduce administrative burdens in clinical practice, aiming to improve both provider efficiency and patient care. The Frontenac Lennox and Addington Ontario Health Team (FLA OHT) has implemented an AI scribe pilot project to assess its effectiveness, usability, and overall impact on healthcare providers' workflow. This evaluation investigates the experiences of healthcare providers using AI scribe technology, examining its impact on administrative efficiency, workflow integration, and provider and patient satisfaction. The study also explores enablers and barriers associated with AI scribe adoption, providing insights into how such tools can be optimized for broader use in primary care settings. Approach: The selection of the AI scribe tool was conducted through a collaborative decision-making process led by the FLA OHT’s Primary Care Digital Health and Technologies Committee. This process included patient engagement and input from member physicians who piloted various tools to assess potential time savings and practice improvements. In year funding was allocated to purchase licenses for 80% of local primary care providers at an enterprise costing rate. A mixed-methods and grounded theory approach was utilized, comprising quantitative usage data and qualitative feedback from healthcare providers through pre- and post-evaluation surveys, periodic check-ins, and semi-structured interviews. Surveys tracked metrics related to workload, ease of use, and impact on patient-provider interactions. Interviews were conducted to gain in-depth insights, coded thematically to capture recurrent themes and experiences across providers from various levels of scribe utilization. Key areas of focus included usability, effectiveness, safety, and change management. Results: Preliminary findings indicate varying levels of comfort with the AI scribe among providers, with most identifying significant time savings and improved workflow efficiency. However, common challenges noted include accuracy issues in specific clinical contexts and the need for consistent vendor support. Providers reported mixed feedback regarding privacy and consent concerns and appreciated the coordinated consent support offered through the OHT. Patient perceptions of the AI scribe were positive with the majority of reports citing an appreciation of enhanced engagement as providers spent less time on documentation. Successful change management strategies, such as peer support and training sessions, were identified as critical enablers for effective implementation. Implications: Initial results suggest that AI scribe technology can alleviate some administrative burdens for healthcare providers, improving efficiency and allowing for a greater focus on patient-centered care. However, enhancements in accuracy and tailored support for specific practice settings are essential to maximize the technology's benefits. The supported implementation of AI scribes was also crucial for engaging local primary care providers in digital technology adoption and created space for conversation around where providers would like to see future innovations to support them and their practice. Further investigation will refine these insights, contributing to a more scalable model for AI scribe deployment across healthcare systems.

title: L’utilisation des scribes IA à travers les disciplines médicales et pourquoi la psychiatrie est en retard : une revue de portée
authors: Daignault, Chloé; Audelin-Rinfret, Justine; Désilets, Marie; Bahremand, Arash; Do, André
abstract: Objective This scoping review aimed to examine the current available literature on the use of artificial intelligence (AI) scribes across all medical fields compared to their use in psychiatry. Methods A scoping review was conducted following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines. Five electronic databases (PubMed, MEDLINE, EMBASE, PsycINFO, and CINAHL) were systematically searched for studies published up to June 2025. Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts according to pre-established eligibility criteria using the PICOS framework. Full-text articles were then assessed for inclusion. Results A total of 1896 records were identified, of which 15 met the inclusion criteria. Most studies were conducted in outpatient, primary care, and procedural settings. Across studies, clinicians generally reported favorable acceptance and perceptions of AI scribes. Findings also suggested improved clinician well-being, reduced documentation time, better workflow efficiency, and positive patient experience. Results on documentation accuracy and quality were mixed. Critically, no eligible studies evaluated the use of AI scribes in psychiatry. Limitations included study heterogeneity, with wide variations in study design, sample size, and evaluation metrics. Conclusion The absence of empirical studies in psychiatry highlights a significant gap in the literature, particularly in contrast to the growing body of research across other medical specialties. Because of its unique clinical, ethical, and relational dimensions, dedicated research is needed to evaluate the feasibility, safety, and ethical implications of implementing AI scribes in psychiatric care.

title: AI Scribe Technology Improves Effciency of Consultations in Dutch Primary Care: A Real-world Observational Pre-post Study
authors: Marco Haak; Y. Zuidwijk; E. de Jong-Gerding; Marco H. Blanker; Henk van der Worp; Anne Martina Maria Loohuis
abstract: BackgroundAdministrative burden contributes substantially to workload and burnout in primary care. AI-based voice-to-note tools (“AI scribes”) may reduce documentation time, but real-world evidence in primary care remains limited. We evaluated the impact of a Dutch-language AI scribe on consultation efficiency in routine primary care. MethodsWe conducted a prospective pre–post pilot study between December, 2024, and May, 2025, in 16 general practices in the province of Drenthe, the Netherlands. General practitioners (GPs) and nurse practitioners (NPs) registered 20 consecutive consultations before and after implementation of an AI scribe integrated with their electronic health record system. The primary outcome was the difference in the proportion of consultation time spent on administration (percentage points, 95% CI). Secondary outcomes were total consultation duration (seconds), administrative time (seconds), and number of clinical issues addressed. Linear mixed-effects models accounted for clustering within clinicians and practices. FindingsNineteen clinicians (14 GPs, five NPs) contributed 719 consultations (379 pre-use; 340 during use). The proportion of consultation time spent on administration decreased by 9,1 percentage points (95% CI −10,5 to −7,7). Administrative time decreased by 100 seconds (95% CI −116 to −84), and total consultation time decreased by 114 seconds (95% CI −176 to −53). The number of clinical issues addressed per consultation did not change (mean difference −0,02, 95% CI −0,10 to 0,05). Among GPs, administrative time proportion decreased from 27,8% to 17,4% (absolute difference −10,6 percentage points). Effects were independent of age and typing proficiency. InterpretationIn routine Dutch general practice, AI-supported documentation substantially reduced administrative workload and overall consultation time without reducing consultation content. Context-specific integration and evaluation after implementation may be key determinants of effectiveness. Larger controlled studies are needed to assess long-term sustainability, quality, patient experience, and cost-effectiveness. FundingNo commercial funding. The regional GP organisation facilitated participation through discounted access to the technology.

title: Evaluating the Usability, Technical Performance, and Accuracy of Artificial Intelligence (AI) Scribes for Primary Care: A Competitive Analysis (Preprint)
authors: Emily Ha; Isabelle Choon-Kon-Yune; LaShawn Murray; Siying Luan; Enid Montague; Onil Bhattacharyya; Payal Agarwal
abstract: BACKGROUND Primary care providers (PCPs) face significant burnout due to increasing administrative and documentation demands, contributing to job dissatisfaction and impacting care quality. Artificial intelligence (AI) scribes have emerged as potential solutions to reduce administrative burden by automating clinical documentation of patient encounters. Although AI scribes are gaining popularity in primary care, there is limited information on their usability, effectiveness, and accuracy. OBJECTIVE This study aimed to develop and apply an evaluation framework to systematically assess the usability, technical performance, and accuracy of various AI scribes used in primary care settings across Canada and the United States. METHODS We conducted a systematic comparison of a suite of AI scribes using competitive analysis methods. An evaluation framework was developed using expert usability approaches and human factors engineering principles, and comprises of 3 domains: usability, effectiveness and technical performance, and accuracy and quality. Audio files from 4 standardized patient encounters were used to generate transcripts and SOAP-format (Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan) medical notes from each AI scribe. A verbatim transcript, detailed case notes, and physician-written medical notes for each audio file served as a benchmark for comparison against the AI-generated outputs. Applicable items were rated on a 3-point Likert scale (1 = poor, 2 = good, 3 = excellent). Additional insights were gathered from clinical experts, vendor questionnaires, and public resources to support usability, effectiveness, and quality findings. RESULTS In total, 6 AI scribes were evaluated, with notable performance differences. Most AI scribes could be accessed via various platforms (n=4) and launched within common electronic medical records (EMRs), though data exchange capabilities were limited. Nearly all AI scribes generated SOAP-format notes in approximately one minute for a 15-minute standardized encounter (n=5), though documentation time increased with encounter length and topic complexity. While all AI scribes produced good to excellent quality medical notes, none were consistently error-free. Common errors included deletion, omission, and SOAP structure errors. Factors such as extraneous conversations and multiple speakers impacted the accuracy of both the transcript and medical note, with some AI scribes producing excellent notes despite minor transcript issues and vice versa. Limitations in usability, technical performance, and accuracy suggest areas for improvement to fully realize AI scribes' potential in reducing administrative burden for PCPs. CONCLUSIONS This study offers one of the first systematic evaluations on the usability, effectiveness, and accuracy of a suite of AI scribes currently used in primary care, providing benchmark data for further research, policy, and practice. While AI scribes show promise in reducing documentation burdens, improvements and ongoing evaluations are essential to ensure safe and effective use. Future studies should assess AI scribe performance in real-world settings across diverse populations to support equitable and reliable application.

title: AI-Scribe in Specialized Rehabilitation: An Explorative Cohort Study of Perceived Usability and Usefulness Among Physicians and Psychologists (Preprint)
authors: Harald Kåre Engan; Ingeborg Landstad; Kari Sand; Ståle Evenshaug; Einar Henjum Halsnes
abstract: BACKGROUND Clinical documentation in specialized, interdisciplinary rehabilitation is often time-consuming and complex, as the underlying issues are persistent and multifaceted. The documentation process may contribute to clinician burnout, job dissatisfaction, and reduced time for patient interaction. Digital scribes based on artificial intelligence (AI) transcribe and summarize clinical notes. These scribes may help reduce documentation burden; however, their usefulness and usability in specialized rehabilitation services remain uninvestigated. OBJECTIVE This study assessed the use of an ambient AI-scribing tool among physicians and psychologists in specialized rehabilitation, focusing on perceived usefulness, usability, note quality, impact on patient interaction, perceptions of time spent on documentation, and documentation-related fatigue. METHODS Over approximately four weeks, physicians and psychologists at nine specialized rehabilitation centers used an ambient AI-scribe tool during clinical consultations. Usability and user experience were assessed using the System Usability Scale (SUS) and a modified Technology Acceptance Model (TAM). Participants rated an AI-generated note using a modified PDQI-9 questionnaire to evaluate documentation quality. Additional questions explored perceived impact on patient interaction, documentation-related fatigue, and general attitudes toward AI technology (AIAS). RESULTS Thirty-one clinicians (18 physicians, 13 psychologists) used the AI-scribe over approximately one month and completed evaluation questionnaires. The mean SUS score was 78.3 (SD = 10.4), with 84.4% scoring above the usability threshold. Perceived usefulness (PU) and ease of use (PEOU) were relatively high (mean PU = 5.65; PEOU = 5.56), and 87% expressed intention to use the AI-scribe in future practice. Most participants (79%) agreed that using the AI-scribe reduced time spent on documentation, while 66% reported a reduced perception of documentation-related fatigue. The quality of AI-generated notes was rated relatively high, with a mean modified PDQI-9 score of 4.3 (SD = 0.3) out of 5. Comprehensibility received the highest rating (M = 4.6, SD = 0.6), while thoroughness scored lowest (M = 3.9, SD = 1.0) among the note quality variables. Approximately 69% and 66% of participants expressed some level of agreement that the AI-scribe enhanced attentiveness and reduced distractions during patient consultations. A few participants reported that some notes were incomplete, lacked biopsychosocial details, and contained inaccuracies CONCLUSIONS This study demonstrated broad acceptance of an AI-based ambient scribe among physicians and psychologists working in specialized rehabilitation. The AI-scribe was generally perceived as valuable, easy to use, and clinically relevant, with high usability scores, strong future use intent, and positive ratings of documentation quality. Most participants reported reduced perceived documentation burden and improved attentiveness during consultations, suggesting a potential for more focused, patient-centered interactions. Some concerns were noted regarding completeness and occasional inaccuracies, highlighting areas for refinement. Future research should explore long-term implementation in routine rehabilitation settings, including effects on workflow, documentation time, note accuracy, and patient experience across diverse clinical roles.

title: Artificial Intelligence (AI) Scribes in Primary Care: A Multi-Country, Mixed-Methods, Simulation-based Workshop Study
authors: Ahmed Alboksmaty; Benedict WJ Hayhoe; Sara Sousi; Geva Greenfield; Thomas Beaney; Ana Luisa Neves
abstract: Background: AI-powered Ambient Voice Technology (AVT) is increasingly being adopted in primary care to support General Practitioners (GPs) with clinical documentation. However, their implementation and influence on care delivery, including the implications of interoperability and cross-system deployment, remain insufficiently explored across different healthcare contexts. This study aims to explore perceptions of the implementation needs and impact of AVT on primary care practice across diverse healthcare systems.<br><br>Methods: A convergent mixed-methods design was used, combining a structured questionnaire with a facilitated group discussion guided by modified Nominal Group Technique principles. Data were collected during an in-person workshop in an international conference, which started with a simulated primary care consultation using an AVT tool. Quantitative data were analysed descriptively, while qualitative data were analysed using a combined deductive–inductive analytical approach. Findings were integrated to generate overall study outcomes.<br><br>Findings: Fifty-four healthcare professionals participated, of whom 83% were GPs, practising in 21 different countries. Most participants (n=46) expressed an intention to use AVT, and approximately four in five perceived them as easy to use without substantial technical support. AVT was viewed as potentially improving efficiency, patient-centredness, and the overall consultation experience, while reducing administrative workload. Participants shared concerns related to ethical, governance, and regulatory requirements across healthcare systems, as well as the variability in electronic health record integration. Patient safety was a key consideration, particularly regarding documentation accuracy and the continued accountability of GPs for final clinical records.<br><br>Interpretation: AVT is widely perceived by primary care clinicians as a potentially transformative intervention for both patients and clinicians. However, its safe, equitable, and effective use depends on context-specific implementation, robust governance frameworks, and careful integration within existing primary care systems.
